title: A 25-Year Study of 32,000 People Found That Quitting Smoking Drops Dementia Risk to the Level of Someone Who Never Smoked.
excerpt: The benefit kicks in after about seven years smoke-free. For South Asian families where elder male smoking is common, the findings are a wake-up call that it is never too late.
body:
The message has always been clear for hearts and lungs: stop smoking. A new study, published in the journal *Neurology* and based on 25 years of data from more than 32,000 adults, now extends that message to the brain. Quitting smoking does not merely slow cognitive decline — it can bring dementia risk back down to the level of someone who never picked up a cigarette.

## The Study

Researchers at a university in China tracked 32,000 adults across two and a half decades, documenting 5,868 cases of dementia along the way. Participants who quit smoking during the study had a significantly lower risk of developing dementia than those who continued. Their risk was comparable to people who had quit before the study began — and, strikingly, to people who had never smoked at all.

The longer someone stayed smoke-free, the more their risk fell. After approximately seven years without cigarettes, the dementia risk of former smokers was statistically indistinguishable from that of lifelong non-smokers. The benefit was strongest among those who gained little or no weight after quitting.

"Our findings suggest that quitting smoking may support long-term brain health, but they also highlight that what happens after quitting matters," said lead researcher Hui Chen.

## Why the Brain Responds

Smoking damages the brain through multiple pathways. It promotes chronic inflammation, generates oxidative stress through unstable molecules called free radicals, and harms the blood vessels that deliver oxygen to the brain. All three mechanisms are linked to cognitive decline and elevated dementia risk.

"The key takeaway is that the brain appears to benefit from smoking cessation at virtually any stage," said Dr Zaid Fadul, a Harvard-trained physician who was not involved in the study. "Importantly, it is rarely 'too late' to quit. While earlier cessation offers the greatest benefit, the body and brain begin recovering soon after smoking stops."

The findings align with a 2025 study in *The Lancet Healthy Longevity* that tracked 4,700 smokers who quit and found that the rate of memory decline slowed by 20 per cent and verbal fluency decline slowed by 50 per cent in the six years following cessation. In practical terms, each year of ageing produced three to four months less memory decline and six months less fluency decline in quitters compared to those who continued.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, these findings carry particular weight. Smoking rates among older South Asian men in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada remain meaningfully higher than the general population. The pattern is generational: many first-generation immigrant men brought the habit from India, Pakistan, or Bangladesh, where smoking prevalence among men has historically exceeded 25 per cent.

Bidi smoking — hand-rolled leaf cigarettes common in India — delivers nicotine and tar at concentrations often exceeding those of manufactured cigarettes. Research from the Global Adult Tobacco Survey shows that India alone has more than 270 million tobacco users, and while the country has made progress through advertising bans and graphic packaging warnings, many men who emigrated decades ago have smoked for 30 or 40 years and assume the damage is irreversible.

This study says otherwise. Seven years of abstinence was enough to erase the statistical difference in dementia risk between quitters and never-smokers.

## What Families Can Do

Dementia is already a growing concern in South Asian families, compounded by the fact that it carries significant stigma in many communities and is often attributed to ageing rather than treated as a medical condition. The evidence now suggests that one of the most effective preventative interventions is also one of the most straightforward: helping a parent or grandparent quit smoking.

Cold turkey remains the most commonly attempted approach and the least effective. Evidence-based options — nicotine patches, prescription medication, and counselling — double or triple success rates. Insurance coverage, including both counselling and medicine, further increases the likelihood of a successful quit, according to a 2020 report by the US Surgeon General.

The conversation does not need to start with lung cancer statistics. For many South Asian elders, the prospect of losing their memory and independence may resonate more deeply than abstract mortality risk. This study provides a concrete, evidence-based reason to have that conversation now.

**Sources:** *Neurology* (2026), The Lancet Healthy Longevity (2025), Fox News Digital / Dr Zaid Fadul interview, American Heart Association, Global Adult Tobacco Survey (WHO)
